content: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) is the recommended approach in areas where it is appropriate, and intermittent preventive treatment for infants (IPTi) should not be used in these regions. Administering IPTi involves crushing a tablet, mixing it with clean water, and giving it to an infant using a spoon, which is not ideal in SMC-targeted areas. In the Sahel sub-region of Africa, most cases of childhood malaria-related illness and death occur during the rainy season. Administering effective malaria treatment at monthly intervals during this period has been shown to prevent illness and death in children. SMC, previously known as intermittent preventive treatment for children, involves the periodic administration of full treatment courses of antimalarial medication to children during the malaria season in areas with highly seasonal transmission. Approximately 25 million children aged 3–59 months could benefit from SMC annually. SMC is typically delivered through mass campaigns, either at fixed points or door-to-door, using trained community health workers. There is limited experience with health facility-based or immunization outreach-based delivery of SMC, although these methods have been used in some cases. However, facility-based approaches alone are less effective in reaching children in remote areas with limited access to health facilities. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends SMC in areas of highly seasonal malaria transmission in the Sahel sub-region where drug resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) is low. A complete treatment course of amodiaquine plus SP (AQ+SP) should be given to children aged 3–59 months at monthly intervals, starting at the beginning of the transmission season, with a maximum of four doses during the malaria season, provided the drugs retain sufficient antimalarial efficacy. Deworming interventions are also critical in many developing countries, where soil-transmitted helminths (STH) affect billions of people, impairing nutritional status. Pregnant women and children are particularly at risk. Deworming drugs, such as single-dose albendazole or mebendazole, are often administered through immunization campaigns. The global target is to eliminate STH-related morbidity in children by 2020 by regularly deworming at least 75% of children in endemic areas. Family planning services remain underutilized in many low-income countries, particularly during the postpartum period, despite high unmet needs. In contrast, child immunization services have high utilization rates. Integrating family planning counseling and services into immunization visits offers an opportunity to address this gap. Studies have shown that integrating family planning with immunization services can be an effective strategy to increase contraceptive use among postpartum women without negatively affecting immunization uptake. HIV testing during immunization visits has also shown high acceptance among mothers, with studies reporting acceptance rates of 90–100%. Integrating early infant diagnosis (EID) of HIV into immunization programs provides an opportunity to identify HIV-exposed and infected infants early, enabling timely initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). WHO recommends HIV testing at key points in the first two years of life, coinciding with immunization schedules, such as at six weeks, nine months, and 18 months. Overall, integrating health interventions such as SMC, deworming, family planning, and HIV testing into immunization programs can improve service delivery, increase coverage, and enhance health outcomes.
